# Detecting viruses and antiviral targets

> *Viruses are too small for the light microscope and multiply only inside living cells, so the
> stains and agar plates that find bacteria miss them. They are detected instead by their nucleic
> acid, their proteins or the antibodies they provoke, and drugs can act only on the few enzymes and
> proteins a virus brings into the cell.*

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Learning objectives
- Explain why viruses are not detected by light microscopy or by culture on agar.
- Match NAATs, viral load, antigen tests, serology and cell culture to what each detects, and state
  what a positive and a negative result can and cannot show.
- Choose a test for a stated clinical question about a viral infection.
- Name the step of the replication cycle that each class of antiviral drug blocks.
- Explain why antiviral drugs are fewer and narrower in range than antibacterial drugs, and why they
  cannot clear a latent virus.
- Explain why HIV infection is treated with a combination of drugs.
:::

## Finding a virus {#sec-vdet-finding}

### Why the bacterial methods fail {#sec-vdet-why}

Two methods that identify most bacteria fail for viruses, and each failure follows from how a virus
is built (see [*How viruses are built and copy
themselves*](virus-structure-replication.qmd#sec-vstr-structure)):

- Most virus particles are smaller than the smallest object a light microscope can resolve, so a
  stain shows nothing useful (compare the Gram stain in [*Detecting bacteria and testing
  susceptibility*](../bacteria/detecting-bacteria.qmd#sec-dbac-microscopy)).
- A virus has no ribosomes and no energy supply of its own, so it cannot grow on agar. Like the
  obligate intracellular bacteria, it multiplies only inside living cells (see [*Detecting bacteria
  and testing susceptibility*](../bacteria/detecting-bacteria.qmd#sec-dbac-culture)).

Electron microscopy can show virus particles, but it needs many of them in the sample and identifies
only the family from the shape, so it has little place in routine diagnosis. Clinical virology
therefore relies on detecting viral molecules and the host's antibodies, the two kinds of method that
work in the same way for every kind of agent (see [*Detecting and controlling
microbes*](../foundations/detection-control.qmd#sec-det-kinds)). Cell culture, the viral counterpart
of growing bacteria, is kept for reference laboratories.

### Methods that detect viruses {#sec-vdet-methods}

Five methods are in routine use. What each detects sets how quickly it answers and what its result can
and cannot show.

| Method | What it detects | Time to result | A positive result shows | What a result cannot show |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| NAAT | Viral DNA or RNA | Hours | The viral genome is in the sample | Whether the virus is still infectious; viral nucleic acid can remain after recovery |
| Quantitative NAAT (viral load) | The amount of viral nucleic acid, usually in blood | Hours | How much virus is present, and whether it is rising or falling | Whether the virus has gone: viral DNA kept inside resting cells is not measured |
| Antigen test | A viral protein | Minutes | Virus is present in large amounts at the site sampled | Absence of infection: a negative result can miss smaller amounts of virus |
| Serology | The patient's antibodies to the virus | Minutes to hours | The person has met the virus, or a vaccine, at some time | Whether the virus is present now; early in infection, antibodies may not yet have formed |
| Cell culture | Infectious virus that multiplies in cultured cells | Days to weeks | Live virus was in the sample | An answer in time for most treatment decisions; many viruses grow poorly or not at all in culture |

NAATs are the usual first test for most acute viral infections, because they are fast and sensitive
and need no living virus. Their limits are those of
every NAAT (see [*Detecting and controlling
microbes*](../foundations/detection-control.qmd#sec-det-molecular)): a positive result shows the
sequence, and a test reports only the viruses it was designed to detect. Influenza virus is detected
in this way on a swab from the nose or throat.

A NAAT can also be made quantitative. The **viral load** is the amount of viral nucleic
acid in a sample, usually plasma, measured by a quantitative NAAT. The trend over time matters more
than a single value: a falling viral load shows that treatment is suppressing replication, and a rise
during treatment suggests that the virus has become resistant or that doses are being missed.

::: {.example}
HIV infection is monitored by repeated viral load measurements. Effective treatment brings HIV RNA in
the blood below the level the test can detect, while the integrated viral DNA remains in resting
CD4 T cells (see [*Viruses and the host*](virus-host.qmd#sec-vhost-persistence)).
:::

An **antigen test** detects a viral protein in a sample, usually with antibodies
fixed to a paper strip that shows a coloured line when the protein binds, and gives a result within
minutes without a laboratory. Nothing is amplified, so an antigen test needs far more virus than a
NAAT to turn positive. A positive result in an ill person is usually reliable; a negative result does
not exclude infection.

::: {.example}
Rapid antigen tests for influenza virus on a nasal swab give a result during a clinic visit, but they
miss a substantial proportion of the infections that a NAAT on the same swab detects.
:::

Serology for viruses follows the rules for reading antibody results that apply to every agent
(see [*Detecting and controlling
microbes*](../foundations/detection-control.qmd#sec-det-serology)): IgM, or a fourfold rise in titre
between paired sera, indicates recent infection, and IgG alone may reflect past infection or
vaccination. For viruses, serology has three main uses:

- Diagnosing an infection after the virus has left the body.
- Establishing immunity, for example after vaccination.
- Diagnosing a lifelong infection, in which antibodies and virus are present together.

HIV infection is the main example of the last use. HIV persists despite the antibody response, so a
positive antibody test in an adult means current infection. Antibodies take some weeks to appear
after infection, and the interval in which an infected person still tests negative is the **window
period**. Detecting a viral protein alongside the antibodies, as HIV tests usually do, shortens the
window period, and a NAAT shortens it further.

In cell culture, virus from a sample is added to layers of cells grown in the laboratory. A virus
that multiplies in them changes or kills the cells in a way visible under the microscope, the
cytopathic effect (see [*Viruses and the host*](virus-host.qmd#sec-vhost-damage)). Culture is slow and
grows only viruses suited to the cells used, so it is rarely used to diagnose an individual patient.
Its advantage, as with bacterial culture, is a living isolate whose properties can be studied.

::: {.example}
Reference laboratories grow influenza virus from samples collected across the world and compare the
circulating strains with those in the current vaccine, to guide the choice of strains for the next
vaccine (see [*How viruses change*](virus-change.qmd#sec-vchg-consequences)).
:::

### Choosing a test {#sec-vdet-choosing}

The choice follows from the clinical question: whether the virus is present now, how much of it there
is, or whether the person has ever met it.

| Clinical question | Best first test | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Does this ill adult have influenza now? | NAAT on a nasal or throat swab | Sensitive, detects current infection, result within hours |
| Is influenza likely, with an answer needed during the visit? | Antigen test | Result within minutes; a negative result does not exclude influenza |
| Has this adult been infected with HIV? | Antibody test combined with detection of a viral protein | HIV persists, so antibodies indicate current infection; the viral protein shortens the window period |
| Is this person's HIV treatment working? | Viral load | A falling or undetectable viral load shows that replication is suppressed |
| Is this health worker immune after vaccination? | Serology for IgG | The antibody response is the question; no virus is present to detect |

::: {.example}
An infant born to a mother with HIV infection carries the mother's antibodies to HIV, because IgG
crosses the placenta and persists in the infant for many months. An antibody test is therefore
positive whether or not the infant is infected, and infection in the infant is diagnosed by a NAAT
for HIV nucleic acid.
:::

## Treating viral infections {#sec-vdet-treat}

### Antiviral targets along the replication cycle {#sec-vdet-targets}

A virus uses the host cell's ribosomes, energy and building blocks, and brings only a few enzymes and
proteins of its own. Antiviral drugs act on these viral molecules, at the steps of the replication
cycle where each one works (see [*How viruses are built and copy
themselves*](virus-structure-replication.qmd#sec-vstr-cycle)).

::: {.flow}
1. Attach
2. Enter
3. Uncoat
4. Copy the genome
5. Assemble
6. Release
:::

Drug classes are named by their target, and each acts at one of these steps:

| Step | Drug class | What the drug blocks | Anchor virus |
|---|---|---|---|
| Attach and enter | Entry and fusion inhibitors | Binding of the virus to the cell, or fusion of the viral envelope with the cell membrane | HIV |
| Copy the genome | Polymerase inhibitors | The viral polymerase that copies the genome | Used against several DNA and RNA viruses |
| Copy the genome | Reverse transcriptase inhibitors | Copying of the RNA genome into DNA by [reverse transcriptase](virus-structure-replication.qmd#sec-vstr-genomes) | HIV |
| Copy the genome | Integrase inhibitors | [Integration](virus-structure-replication.qmd#sec-vstr-genomes) of the DNA copy into a host chromosome | HIV |
| Assemble | Protease inhibitors | Cutting of long viral proteins into their working parts, so new virions form but cannot infect | HIV |
| Release | Neuraminidase inhibitors | Release of new virions from the cell surface, by blocking [neuraminidase](virus-structure-replication.qmd#sec-vstr-structure) | Influenza virus |

::: {.example}
New influenza virions bud from the cell but stay held to its surface by haemagglutinin until
neuraminidase cuts the receptors that hold them. A neuraminidase inhibitor leaves the virions stuck
to the cell, so the infection spreads more slowly to neighbouring cells.
:::

These drugs stop new virus being made or released; they do not destroy virus already made, and the
infected cells are cleared by the immune response. They therefore help most while the virus is still
multiplying rapidly, which in influenza means early in the illness.

### Why antiviral drugs are few {#sec-vdet-few}

Antibacterial drugs act on structures that bacteria have and human cells lack, such as peptidoglycan
and the 70S ribosome (see [*How bacteria are built and get
energy*](../bacteria/bacteria-build-energy.qmd#sec-bact-glance)). A virus offers far fewer such
targets, and three consequences follow:

- A drug that blocked the host's ribosomes or energy supply would harm the host, so antiviral drugs
  must act on viral enzymes and proteins, and a virus encodes only a few of them.
- Viral enzymes differ between families, so most antiviral drugs act on one virus or one family,
  whereas one antibacterial drug can treat many species. The virus usually has to be identified
  before a drug is chosen.
- A latent virus offers no target. Its genome sits in the cell without being copied, so drugs that
  block copying, assembly or release have nothing to act on (see [*Viruses and the
  host*](virus-host.qmd#sec-vhost-persistence)).

::: {.example}
In HIV infection, the integrated viral DNA persists in resting CD4 T cells that make no virus. Drugs
suppress replication in active cells but leave this reservoir untouched, so treatment continues for
life.
:::

Antibacterial drugs have no effect on viral replication (see [*How viruses are built and copy
themselves*](virus-structure-replication.qmd#sec-vstr-targets)). In a viral illness they help only
when a bacterial infection follows, as bacterial pneumonia can follow influenza.

Because antiviral drugs are few and narrow, and act only while a virus is replicating, vaccines are
the main means of preventing viral infection (see [*Detecting and controlling
microbes*](../foundations/detection-control.qmd#sec-det-prevent)).

### Resistance and combination therapy {#sec-vdet-resistance}

Many viral polymerases, reverse transcriptase among them, copy without proofreading, so a large viral
population already contains variants with mutations in a drug's target before treatment begins (see
[*How viruses change*](virus-change.qmd#sec-vchg-mutation)). A single drug suppresses the susceptible
virus and leaves these variants to multiply, the same selection that produces resistance in bacteria
(see [*How viruses change*](virus-change.qmd#sec-vchg-consequences)).

**Combination therapy** is treatment with two or more drugs at once, acting on different targets, so
that a variant resistant to one drug is still suppressed by the others. A variant that escapes every
drug needs several resistance mutations at the same time, which is far less likely than one.

::: {.example}
HIV infection is treated with a combination of drugs, usually from two or more classes, such as
reverse transcriptase inhibitors together with an integrase inhibitor. Missed doses let drug levels
fall while the virus is still exposed to some drug, the conditions that select resistant variants.
:::

When the viral load rises during treatment, resistance is looked for by sequencing the viral genes
that encode the drug targets. This is the viral counterpart of susceptibility testing in bacteria (see
[*Detecting bacteria and testing susceptibility*](../bacteria/detecting-bacteria.qmd#sec-dbac-mic)),
and it needs no culture.
